title: Accommodation vs. Modification — Primer
description: Foundational distinction between accommodations (change HOW the student accesses/responds) and modifications (change WHAT the student learns). Use when deciding whether a proposed change to a lesson keeps content equivalent (accommodation) or alters expectations (modification). Modifications may impact graduation requirements; accommodations do not.

source.name: Composite — Wikipedia (IEP, Special Education) and Understood.org video transcript

key_distinctions.definition: A reasonable adjustment to teaching practices so the student learns the SAME material in a more accessible format. Does not alter content. Common categories: presentation (how info is shown), response (how the student answers), setting (where the work happens), scheduling (timing of work).
examples: Listening to an audiobook while reading the same printed text
Sitting at the front of the room
Typing answers instead of handwriting them
Taking a test in a quieter room

key_distinctions.definition: A change to WHAT the student is expected to learn, demonstrate, or be assessed on. Alters content, mastery level, or assessment criteria. May impact graduation eligibility — verify with the IEP team before applying broad modifications.
examples: Substituting a shorter, easier book for the assigned text
Reducing the number of problems on a math worksheet (when the reduction changes what is mastered, not just the volume)
Modifying a grading rubric to assess different standards
Skipping a curriculum section deemed inappropriate for the student
Working on identifying hours while the rest of the class is learning to read minutes

key_distinctions.definition: Adaptation of content, methodology, or delivery of instruction designed by a credentialed special-education teacher to meet the unique needs of a student. Goes deeper than accommodations — affects HOW the teacher teaches, not just how the student accesses content.
examples: Multi-sensory phonics instruction for a student with dyslexia (Orton-Gillingham)
Direct, explicit teaching of a reading-comprehension strategy
Use of manipulatives to teach abstract math concepts
Pre-teaching key vocabulary before a content lesson

decision_guide.title: When to use which
rules: If the change preserves the same learning objective and mastery expectation, it is an accommodation.
If the change alters the learning objective, the mastery expectation, or the assessment criteria, it is a modification.
Accommodations are the default — start there and only modify when the IEP authorizes it (the IEP's Modifications section explicitly lists what's allowed).
Modifications must be documented in the IEP. Generating a modification beyond what the IEP authorizes is outside scope.
When in doubt, frame the proposal as an accommodation; flag it for the IEP team if it edges toward modification.

common_pitfalls.text: Applying blanket accommodations (extra time, sit in front) without tying them to the specific cognitive or achievement deficit they address. Each accommodation should connect to a specific present-level finding.

Stacking modifications without considering graduation impact. A student receiving reading-content modifications throughout middle and high school may not meet diploma requirements. The IEP team must consider this.

Implementing accommodations or modifications that single the student out in front of peers (e.g., visibly different worksheet, separate desk). Look for adaptations the student can use without peer attention — bone-conduction headphones for audio text, generic-looking graphic organizer, etc.
